Some large grids are regular rectangular lattices: horizontal/vertical separator lines have a scaffold color, cells have uniform background fill, and exceptional colors appear at separator intersections. Decode each rectangle between consecutive separator rows and columns: if its four corner intersection values are all the same exceptional color (not scaffold), that color is the output cell; otherwise use the interior/base fill color. Then crop away outer rows/columns that are entirely base fill, keeping the bounding box of exceptional decoded cells. For this instance, separator rows r=0,4,8,12,16,20,24; cols c=4,9,14,19,24; base fill=3, scaffold=4. Decoded 6x4 matrix was [[3,3,3,3],[3,3,9,3],[3,3,3,3],[3,2,3,7],[3,3,3,3],[3,7,3,1]], cropping to active bounds yielded [[3,9,3],[3,3,3],[2,3,7],[3,3,3],[7,3,1]]. Demonstrations validate: decode marker lattice, crop inactive base-colored borders. In some inputs separators have varying spacings/offsets; identify periodic separator rows/cols from repeating scaffold first. Do not confuse scaffold color with fill color; output defaults to cell interior fill, not separator. In demo1 a single rectangle with four equal corner markers decoded to 1x1 marker. In other examples output size matches active bounding rectangle.', path='arc', scope='global', reference={}, arguments={}, metadata={}, source='agent', created_at='2026-10-21T04:57:15.609523+00:00', updated_at='2026-10-21T04:57:15.609538+00:00', version=1), HarnessEntry(id='arc_recolor_matching_shape_across_l_divider_task_25100e09', kind='memory', title='ARC recolor matching shape across L divider (task-25100e09)', content='Continual-ARC task-25100e09: A long 1-cell-thick L-shaped line marks the recolor color. Recolor the matching component on the side opposite the L’s arms with the L line’s color; leave its matching counterpart unchanged. In the test grid, color-5 L ran upward in col17 and right along row5. A color-7 component at rows0–3, cols20–23 had shape rows: #### / #.## / ..## / ..##. The identical shape in color6 lay at rows5–8, cols7–10; recolor those 11 cells to 5. Distractors included many other 6/7 components. Demos confirm selecting a repeated congruent component (e.g. demo7 had a color-5 5-cell shape matching color2, and changed one to the L color; demo8 changed a 3-cell L matching another such L). Use 4-connectivity and normalize component shapes under translation; compare exact cell pattern. Then use L orientation/position to choose the copy opposite the arms. A likely governing pattern is one repeated shape pair, with target copy on the far/opposite side of the L. Caveat: examples are varied, so verify exact shape duplicates and spatial side before recoloring.', path='general', scope='global', reference={}, arguments={}, metadata={}, source='agent', created_at='2026-10-21T04:02:21.059633+00:00', updated_at='2026-10-21T04:02:21.059649+00:00', version=1), HarnessEntry(id='arc_two_panel_matching_shared_color_cells', kind='memory', title='ARC two-panel matching shared-color cells', content='Continual-ARC task-94354d14 demonstrations showed grids split by a full uniform divider row or column into equal panels. Sparse same-color diagonal strokes encode a fully periodic grid. Determine orientation from diagonal slope and period from distinct colors/phases. For downward-left diagonals, cells share residues of (row+column) modulo N; fill every cell by the color assigned to its diagonal residue.
